description: Three-person team from Sivas, Türkiye, new to NASA Space Apps: an aeronautical engineering senior (propulsion, combustion, MATLAB, Python), an electrical and electronics engineering student (data pipelines, interfaces) and a robotics and AI graduate (machine learning). Our challenge: Flame in Freefall. We aim to build an AI fire safety tool from NASA's microgravity combustion data.
summary:
EarthEar turns NASA Earth observations into sound, so anyone, including blind and low-vision people, can explore our changing planet by ear. Pick any place on Earth by voice ("Earth, go to Canada"), keyboard or touch, and a radar sweep circles it: direction becomes stereo position, distance becomes a softer, muffled sound, and the data value becomes loudness and density. Each layer has its own "sound world": Saharan dust sounds like a sandstorm, warm ocean like gentle waves with a saxophone, city lights like an urban hum. A music layer generated from the data shifts between major and minor with the region's stress level.

To answer the Earth Information Jukebox challenge honestly, we do not turn pixel colors directly into notes. We read each NASA Scientific Visualization Studio colorbar with image processing, convert colors back into physical values (°C, aerosol optical depth, etc.) and validate them against independent NASA MERRA-2 data (r ≈ 0.97). EarthEar is fully voice-controlled, works with screen readers and keyboard, includes a narrated 7-day NASA GEOS-FP weather forecast, and runs in any modern browser in English and Turkish.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

EarthEar is a voice-first, accessible web app that lets people hear NASA Earth science data. The user chooses any place on Earth; a radar sweep turns around it and every data cell it passes becomes sound:

- direction → stereo pan (left/right)

- distance → quieter and more muffled

- value → loudness and density

- layer → its own "sound world" (auditory icons): dust = sandstorm, ocean temperature = waves + saxophone, night lights = city hum, vegetation = leaves and birds, surface temperature = icy wind ↔ cicadas, lightning = thunder

A data-driven music layer adds mood (major/minor from a regional stress score, tempo from intensity). There are no random values: the same data always gives the same sound.

HOW IT WORKS (image processing → measurement → sound)

1. Download NASA SVS visualizations and their colorbars (e.g. SVS 3912 sea surface temperature, SVS 5147 surface temperature, SVS 5669 aerosols).

2. Read the colorbar pixels to build a 128-step color → value table; colors that map to two values are flagged.

3. Georeference each frame; control points (Sivas, Tokyo, Lagos) match within about 1 pixel (~15 km).

4. Map every pixel to the nearest scale color → a physical value on a 1° grid, which the radar sonifies.

Validation against independent NASA MERRA-2 data: r = 0.966 (air temperature), r = 0.978 (sea surface temperature); OCO-2 CO₂ cross-check r = 0.976. Every layer was audited (suitable / suspect / excluded); layers that failed (e.g. fire and CO estimates, duplicated variables) were removed, and missing cells stay "no data" instead of being invented. Each layer card shows its source.

ACCESSIBILITY

- Hands-free voice control with the wake word "Earth"/"Dünya", or hold Space to talk; 242 countries, continents and oceans, including Turkish grammar suffixes ("Kanada'ya git").

- "What am I hearing?" gives a spoken summary of the current place and value.

- Full keyboard use, screen-reader announcements (ARIA live regions), high-contrast mode, adjustable speech rate, English and Turkish.

- Meteorologist mode: a narrated 7-day forecast from NASA GEOS-FP, with the weather sound starting before the narration.

IMPACT

At least 2.2 billion people live with a vision impairment (WHO). Earth science is mostly shared as images, maps and color scales that screen readers cannot read. EarthEar opens NASA's Earth stories to them, and gives classrooms, museums and outreach events a multisensory way to explore climate data.

TOOLS

TypeScript, React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, three.js (3D globe), Web Audio API (sound engine), Web Speech API (speech recognition and synthesis), Node.js and Python data scripts (NASA Earthdata/OPeNDAP), FastAPI + PostgreSQL backup API, Netlify/Vercel hosting. Static data files let the app work offline.

CREATIVITY

Instead of mapping colors to notes, EarthEar recovers the real measurement behind each NASA visualization and lets the user steer through it with their voice: "Earth, go to the Sahara… what am I hearing?"

TEAM

Team Kangalactico (Sivas, Türkiye): Tugay Demirci (Aeronautical Engineering student), Taha Öztürk (Computer Engineering student), Ceyhun Pehlivanoğlu (Robotics & AI Technician).

USE OF SUPER INTELLIGENCE

We used Claude (Anthropic) as a coding assistant for the web app and data-processing scripts, and to help draft text and slides. The background music in the demo video was synthesized by AI-written code. All data comes from NASA sources listed below; no images in the project were AI-generated (globe imagery is NASA Blue Marble and NASA SVS; screenshots are of our own app). Code repository: https://github.com/aetugay/Kangalactico
